1 · The zoomed out view

Lines follow the streets now.

Zoomed out, the map drew each block as a straight line from one end to the other. Boston's blocks curve, so 407 lines cut 10 m or more off the street, 41 of them over 50 m, up to 168 m. Each block now draws its real line at every zoom. The ones that strayed most:

2 · Pedestrian streets

Off the parking map.

10 blocks on the sweeping schedule are pedestrian streets on the map: Downtown Crossing and Faneuil Hall Marketplace. The sweepers clean them, but there is no curb to park at, and where the Curb Lab read the signs, they say no stopping. They are left off the map.

How we checked

Every block, sampled every 3 m.

Each block's line (a City street centerline) is sampled every 3 m against the streets the map is drawn from (OpenStreetMap). A point counts as on a street within 7 m of a street for cars (10 m for a major road, 15 m for one with the block's own name). A block that is mostly on a pedestrian way, or mostly on no street at all, is left off the map, unless the Curb Lab's signs post parking on it. The checks run every time the Boston data is rebuilt, and each decision is written down with its numbers.

Data notes for the City: the schedule spells 10 street names differently from the street list (above), and 10 scheduled blocks are pedestrian streets. Where the Curb Lab read a street cleaning sign, it gives a different day or hour than the schedule on 358 of 2,129 curb sides, and on 227 sides its weeks are the ones the schedule gives the other side of the street.
